title: Two Stories about Flying
book: NCERT First Flight: Textbook in English for Class X
subject: english_literature
author: Liam O'Flaherty; Frederick Forsyth
syllabus_note: CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184): First Flight prose, Chapter 3 (His First Flight; The Black Aeroplane). Assessed through extracts (5 marks), short answers in 40-50 words (3 marks) and long answers in 100-120 words (6 marks).

blocks.title: The edge of a cliff, the edge of a storm
blocks.body:
A young seagull stands on a cliff ledge, too afraid to jump. A pilot flies into black storm clouds, his compass spinning and his radio dead.

Both stories are about **flying** and about **fear**. In one, a hungry bird finds its wings; in the other, a pilot is guided home by a plane that, it seems, was never there.

blocks.title: The writers
blocks.body:
**Liam O'Flaherty** was an Irish writer known for stories about animals and nature on the Aran Islands, where seagulls nest on high cliffs.

**Frederick Forsyth** is a British novelist, once a pilot in the Royal Air Force, famous for thrillers such as The Day of the Jackal. The Black Aeroplane is a short mystery told in the first person.
blocks.future: Pilots, mountaineers and athletes all face 'first flights'. Learning to act in spite of fear is a life skill.

blocks.question: The young seagull flies only when he is very hungry. What does this suggest?
options: Sometimes a strong need pushes us past our fear
He never wanted to fly at all
blocks.explanation: Hunger was stronger than fear, so he dived at the fish and found his wings.

blocks.title: What happens in the story
blocks.body:
**Alone on the ledge.** The young seagull is alone on his ledge. The day before, his **two brothers and his sister**, whose wings were far shorter than his own, had run to the brink, flapped their wings and flown away. He had tried, but the great expanse of sea below frightened him; he felt his wings would never support him, so he ran back to the little hole under the ledge.

**Taunted and scolded.** His father and mother came round calling to him, **scolding** him and **threatening** to let him starve on the ledge unless he flew. Now his family is on the plateau opposite: brothers and sister lying down, his father preening his feathers, his mother looking at him. He has had nothing to eat since the previous nightfall and is **hungry**.

**The trick with the fish.** His mother picks up a piece of fish and flies across towards him. She halts just opposite him, legs hanging limp, wings still, the fish almost within reach. Then, **maddened by hunger**, he dives at the fish with a scream.

**Flying!** He falls, and a monstrous terror seizes him, but only for a minute. His wings spread outwards; the wind rushes against his breast; he is **flying**. His mother swoops past him, his father flies over him screaming, and his brothers and sister fly around him. He is no longer afraid.

**The sea.** He lands on the **green sea**. His legs sink into it; he is frightened at first, but then his belly touches the water and he floats. His family lands around him, praising him and offering him scraps of dog-fish. **He had made his first flight.**

blocks.question: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly?
options: his parents did not want him to fly
he thought his wings would not support him over the vast sea
his wings were shorter than his brothers'
blocks.explanation: Fear, not weakness, kept him on the ledge.
option_feedback: His wings were longer than theirs.

blocks.question: What finally made the young seagull fly?
options: hunger: he dived at the fish his mother held out
a strong wind blew him off
blocks.explanation: 'The sight of the food maddened him.'

blocks.title: What happens in the story
blocks.body:
**Going home.** The narrator, a pilot, is flying his old **Dakota** aeroplane over France back to England, at about **1.30 in the morning**, dreaming of his holiday and an **English breakfast**. He calls **Paris Control**, which tells him to turn twelve degrees west.

**'I'll take the risk.'** Ahead he sees huge **black storm clouds**. He could fly back to Paris, but he wants to get home, so he decides to take the risk and flies into the storm.

**Lost in the storm.** Inside the clouds everything is black. The **compass** turns round and round and is dead; the **radio** is dead too. He can see nothing and cannot contact anyone. He is lost, with very little fuel left.

**The black aeroplane.** Suddenly he sees another aeroplane with **no lights** on its wings, flying next to him. Its pilot waves, as if to say 'Follow me'. The narrator follows him through the storm with enough fuel for only a few minutes. Then the clouds clear, and he sees two lines of **runway lights**. He lands safely, and the black aeroplane is gone.

**The mystery.** In the control centre he asks a woman who the other pilot was. She looks at him strangely: **'Black aeroplane? There are no other aeroplanes flying tonight. Yours was the only one I could see on the radar.'** So who helped him reach the airport without a compass, a radio or fuel? The story ends with this question.

blocks.title: The two stories side by side
blocks.body:
| | His First Flight | The Black Aeroplane |
|---|---|---|
| **Who flies** | a young seagull | an experienced pilot in an old Dakota |
| **The problem** | fear of the first flight | a storm, dead instruments and almost no fuel |
| **Who helps** | his mother, by tempting him with a piece of fish | a mysterious black aeroplane with no lights |
| **Turning point** | hunger makes him dive at the fish | he follows the black aeroplane through the clouds |
| **Ending** | he flies, lands on the sea, and is praised by his family | he lands safely, but control says no other plane was flying |
| **Message** | courage comes from facing fear; we sometimes need a push | help may come when we least expect it; mystery remains |

blocks.question: What was 'the risk' the narrator decided to take?
options: flying into the storm instead of returning to Paris
blocks.explanation: He wanted to get home for breakfast.

blocks.question: Why did the woman in the control centre look at the narrator strangely?
options: he had landed at the wrong airport
no other aeroplane was flying that night; only his was on the radar
blocks.explanation: His question about a black aeroplane made no sense to her.
option_feedback: She was puzzled by his question.
He was the pilot of the Dakota.

blocks.title: Words and expressions to know
blocks.body:
| Word or phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ledge** | a narrow shelf of rock on a cliff |
| **brink** | the edge of a steep place |
| **preening** | cleaning and arranging feathers with the beak |
| **taunting** | mocking, teasing to provoke |
| **cajole** | to persuade by coaxing |
| **maddened by hunger** | driven wild by hunger |
| **swoop** | to fly down quickly |
| **plateau** | a flat, raised area of land |
| **Dakota** | a type of old propeller aeroplane |
| **Paris Control** | the air-traffic control centre in Paris |
| **fuel gauge** | the instrument that shows how much fuel is left |

**Style:** His First Flight is told in the **third person** and shows the bird's feelings closely. The Black Aeroplane is told in the **first person** in short, tense sentences, which build suspense and end in a **mystery**.

blocks.question: 'Preening' means:
blocks.explanation: The father was preening the feathers on his white back.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Seagull: Fear → Hunger → Fish → Fall → Fly → Float.**
- **Pilot: Breakfast → Storm → Dead compass and radio → Black plane → Runway → 'No other plane'.**
- **Brothers and sister: two brothers, one sister; wings shorter than his.**
- **Time and plane: 1.30 a.m., old Dakota, Paris Control.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying the seagull's wings were too short: his wings were **longer** than his siblings'; he lacked confidence.
2. Saying his father pushed him: **hunger** made him dive at the fish.
3. Saying the pilot crashed or landed on the sea: he landed safely on a runway.
4. Explaining the black aeroplane as a fact: the story leaves it a **mystery**; give your view but call it a possibility.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Ask: 'Who flew the black aeroplane?' Let groups argue for four answers (a ghost pilot, a guardian angel, the pilot's imagination, a real plane missed by radar), each using details from the story.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Think of something you were afraid to try for the first time (swimming, cycling, speaking on stage). What or who helped you do it?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **A Letter to God (Ch 1):** help also comes from an unseen source.
- **The Ball Poem:** learning to face loss on one's own.
- **Physics:** how wings give lift; why pilots depend on the compass and radio.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
Compare the young seagull and the narrator of The Black Aeroplane. Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Both face fear while flying, but in opposite ways. The young seagull is afraid of his very first flight: the vast sea below makes him think his wings will not hold him, and he stays on the ledge while his family taunts him. Only hunger, when his mother holds out a piece of fish, makes him dive and discover he can fly. The pilot, on the other hand, is experienced and confident, even too confident: he takes the risk of flying into a storm to reach home for breakfast. When his compass and radio fail, he is lost, and only a mysterious black aeroplane guides him to safety. One story shows that we grow by facing fear; the other that help can come from where we least expect it.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- His First Flight: a young seagull, afraid to fly, is left alone on a ledge; hungry, he dives at a fish held by his mother, falls, and finds he can fly. He lands on the sea and his family praises him.
- The Black Aeroplane: a pilot flying a Dakota home to England at night flies into a storm; his compass and radio die. A black aeroplane with no lights guides him to a runway. Control says no other plane was flying.
- Themes: fear and courage, family support, risk, and the mystery of unseen help.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- Name the story you are writing about in every answer; the chapter has two.
- For 'Who helped the narrator?', give your opinion and support it with two details (no lights, waved, vanished, not on radar).
- In long answers on the seagull, use the stages: fear, taunts, hunger, the dive, flight, landing on the sea.

blocks.front: Why could the young seagull not fly at first?
blocks.back: He was afraid; the vast sea below made him think his wings would not support him.

blocks.front: How did his mother get him to fly?
blocks.back: She flew towards him with a piece of fish and stopped just out of reach; maddened by hunger, he dived at it.

blocks.front: What failed in the pilot's aeroplane during the storm?
blocks.back: The compass and the radio; and his fuel was almost finished.

blocks.front: What did the woman at control say about the black aeroplane?
blocks.back: 'There are no other aeroplanes flying tonight. Yours was the only one I could see on the radar.'
